cases.name: apply-crash-leaves-rows-and-old-files
cases.notes: spec/store §5.7: the process dies after COMMIT and before the file half. The api commit and both revisions are durable, both files still hold the previous revision, and one `write` row per document records what each file must become (rev_id = the new revision, rendered_hash = its bytes). The files lag the store legitimately: the runner's file check exempts a path with a pending row.

cases.name: apply-crash-then-materialize-finishes
cases.notes: The same crash, then `materialize` replays both rows from `reconstruct at rev_id` (§6.2): both files carry the new revision, the rows are gone, and no commit was added — the api intent (actor, reason, known ids) was never lost.

cases.name: crash-then-observe-of-stale-file-is-foreign
cases.notes: §5.7 gate rule, the subtle case: after the crash the file on disk still holds the PREVIOUS revision's bytes. An observation of them does not hash to `rendered_hash`, so to the gate they are foreign bytes — indistinguishable from a human who reverted the file — and the file wins: an observed commit of the old bytes lands, the row is deleted in that commit's transaction, and the api revision stays in history (not reverted silently; superseded by an observed one). This is why the materializer, not the observation, is the recovery point: the sweep runs step 0 BEFORE it walks the disk.

cases.name: crash-then-observe-of-new-bytes-is-foreign
cases.notes: After the crash a human edits the file to new bytes: the observation ingests them (file wins) and the row goes with that commit.

cases.name: crash-then-observe-of-rendered-bytes-echoes
cases.notes: After the crash the file is observed holding exactly the bytes the row names (another materializer, or a human writing the same): the observation confirms the intent — an echo, no commit — and deletes the row.

cases.name: crash-then-gone-member-is-not-a-deletion
cases.notes: A gone member whose path has a pending `write` row is not tombstoned: the materializer still owes the file. Outcome `{ deleted: false }`, nothing minted, row kept, document live.

cases.name: crash-then-materialize-keeps-foreign-file
cases.notes: A materializer never overwrites bytes it does not recognise: after the crash a human edits the file, `materialize` writes nothing (`materialized: []`) and keeps the row; the next observation lets the file win and clears the row.

cases.name: crash-then-second-request-materializes-first
cases.notes: A later request touching the path replays the pending row in its phase (a) before reading the file, so the stale file is brought to the committed revision instead of being read back as a human edit (which would have been a `sync_conflict` reverting the first intent). The second request then commits and materializes normally.

cases.name: create-crash-then-materialize-writes
cases.notes: `docs_create` records a `write` row for a document with no previous bytes; `materialize` writes the file where the path is absent.

cases.name: set-meta-crash-then-materialize-writes
cases.notes: `docs_set_meta` is a `write` row like `apply`: the file still holds the pre-patch bytes after the crash; `materialize` writes the patched revision over them.

cases.name: delete-crash-then-materialize-unlinks-unchanged
cases.notes: `docs_delete` records a `remove` row with the deleted revision's rendered hash; after the crash the file lingers; `materialize` unlinks it because it still holds those bytes. Nothing is pooled (an intentional delete).

cases.name: delete-crash-then-materialize-keeps-foreign-file
cases.notes: The `remove` row names the bytes it is safe to unlink. A file a human rewrote after the delete committed is not those bytes: `materialize` leaves it (untracked now — the next sweep re-creates the path) and clears the row.

cases.name: delete-crash-then-observe-of-lingering-file-echoes
cases.notes: Observing the lingering file of a crashed delete: the bytes are the ones the `remove` row names, so the observation is an echo of the tombstoned document (no re-creation) and the row STAYS — only a materializer unlinks; the observe path never writes or removes a file.

cases.name: move-crash-then-materialize-renames
cases.notes: `docs_move` records a `rename` row at the destination (from_path = the old path, rendered_hash = the moved document's current revision). After the crash the file is still at the old path; `materialize` renames it.

cases.name: move-self-link-crash-then-materialize-rewrites
cases.notes: A self-linking moved document is a retarget source: its `rename` row carries the retargeted revision's hash. `materialize` renames the old file and, finding it holds the previous revision, writes the new bytes under the new path.

cases.name: move-crash-then-materialize-writes-when-source-gone
cases.notes: The rename fallback: the old file vanished after the crash; `materialize` writes `reconstruct at rev_id` at the destination.
